# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-17 (Extended v131)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826. **Current narrative point (Spring Year 5—Louis Philippe's reign)**: Paris—Gorbeau house (50-52, Salpêtrière district); Rue de la Verrerie (Courfeyrac's residence); Faubourg Saint-Antoine; Faubourg Saint-Marceau; wine-shops (Seven Billiards on Rue des Mathurins-Saint-Jacques; Corinthe on Rue Mondétour; Richefeu's at Barrière du Maine; Café Musain); schools; English provincial towns (Dunstead harbor town, Staveford, Kelmere, Torton, Ostcombe, Ravenmere, Kelford, Yarlby, Gulhaven, Wilwick, Wilholt, Quenford). **Environmental details**: Frost silvered hedges overnight; chalked crooked sun on forge wall; rain threatened; wind carries salt/tar scent; bees hum in lavender; children chase hoop down lane; road ruts and puddles after thaw; smoke from chimneys lies flat; gulls quarrel over fish heads in harbor/steps; bells ring for vespers; light goes early; river up in spring; baker's boy often late; lines at oven grow long. Dogs bark at nothing. Clouds predicted rain, wrongly.

## Primary Locations
**GORBEAU HOUSE**: 50-52 Salpêtrière district. **JONDRETTE DEN**: Abject, fetid. Furniture: straw chair, infirm table, two pallets, straw beds. Walls: leprous, seamed, charcoal sketches, moisture. Fireplace with red-hot brazier. Dormer window (four broken panes). Colored engraving "THE DREAM" (Napoleon on blue column). **Wooden panel—Battle of Waterloo**: sergeant rescuer (Thénardier) carrying colonel victim (Pontmercy). Rope-ladder with hooks, verdigris candlestick.

**WINE-SHOPS & MEETING PLACES**: Centers of revolutionary fermentation. **Seven Billiards (Rue des Mathurins-Saint-Jacques)** and **Café Rue Saint-Hyacinthe**: student rallying points. **Corinthe (Rue Mondétour)**: young men assemble; secret and public meetings. **Richefeu's (Barrière du Maine)**: marble-workers, painters, journeymen sculptors meet 12-1 o'clock; cooling off, playing dominoes. **Café Musain**: Société des Amis de l'A B C affiliated to Mutualists and Cougourde of Aix.

**PARISIAN FIELD (DUNSTEAD area)**: Green meadow with tightly stretched lines, rags drying in wind, old market-gardener's house (Louis XIII era), great roof with dormer windows, dilapidated palisades, water amid poplar-trees. Horizon shows Panthéon, Deaf-Mutes pole, Val-de-Grâce (black, squat, fantastic), Notre Dame towers.

**PRISONS**: La Force (Bâtiment-Neuf or court Saint-Bernard; robbers call it Fosse-aux-Lions—Lion's Ditch; wall covered with scales, leprosy; old rusty iron door to ancient chapel; dormitories for ruffians; Charlemagne courtyard with sutler's window; fever ward with twenty-eight beds). Les Madelonettes. Salpêtrière.

## Marius Pontmercy: Psychological and Financial Crisis
**Identity and background**: Baron Marius Pontmercy, twenty years old; three years estranged from grandfather. **Paternal legacy**: Colonel's instruction regarding Waterloo sergeant Thénardier. Recognized Thénardier in Waterloo painting.

**The Ambush Crisis (resolved with escape)**: Jondrette/Thénardier plotted extortion via Cosette. M. Leblanc escaped: unscrewed coin piece, used as saw to cut cords, brandished red-hot chisel above head emitting threatening glow. **While red-hot iron sank into smoking wound, impassive and almost august, he fixed on Thénardier his beautiful glance, in which there was no hatred, and where suffering vanished in serene majesty.** Dashed from window. Javert positioned outside with men; took action before Marius's signal. Thénardier woman hurled enormous paving-stone at Javert's head; Javert ducked; stone struck wall. Javert bore off prisoners in three hackney-coaches.

**Marius's aftermath (April Year 4)**: Relocated to Courfeyrac at Rue de la Verrerie for political reasons; paid quarterly rent, vacated hovel. Two reasons: (1) horror of wicked poor man development; (2) avoid lawsuit testimony against Thénardier. Recognized M. Leblanc as Monsieur Fabre (Cosette's biological father). Cosette believed Valjean her father, became convent scholar.

**Current financial crisis (Spring Year 5)**: **First time in life, Marius borrowed five francs from Courfeyrac.** Poverty returned; felt icy breath. Discontinued work—dangerous habit vanishing, difficult to resume. Old coat becoming impossible; new coat growing old; shirts wearing out; hat wearing out; boots giving out.

**Psychological state—Reverie vs. Reason**: Passion precipitated him into chimæras without object or bottom. Lost faculty of working and moving firmly toward fixed goal, but endowed with more clear-sightedness and rectitude than ever. Judgment almost wholly disassociated from hope. **Happy, even in midst of anguish, is he to whom God has given a soul worthy of love and of unhappiness!**

**Marius and Cosette relationship—Memory and hope**: She—that was Marius's whole thought. One sweet idea alone left: she had loved him; her glance told him so; she did not know his name, but she knew his soul. Pure, impersonal, ideal reveries fell upon notebook. He called this "writing to her." **Periodical five francs a double riddle**: to Courfeyrac who lent, to unknown recipient who received them.

## Enjolras and Revolutionary Leadership (Spring Year 5)
**Enjolras as nexus of fermentation**: Believed moment at hand: people taking possession of right; revolution majestically taking France. Furnace being heated. Had powder train of friends scattered all over Paris.

**Composed network**: Collaborators include Combeferre (philosophical, penetrating eloquence), Feuilly (cosmopolitan enthusiasm), Courfeyrac (dash), Bahorel (smile), Jean Prouvaire (melancholy), Joly (science), Bossuet (sarcasms). Created sort of electric spark taking fire nearly everywhere.

## Jean Valjean
Valjean integrated as convent assistant gardener; inhabits old garden hut with Fauchelevent. Spiritual transformation complete. Fauchelevent sole ally aware of full presence.

## Revolutionary Fermentation and Secret Societies (Spring Year 5)
**Public agitation and cartridge-making (April Year 4)**: Workmen openly proclaim cartridge-making. Police raids: April 5, arrested Pardon while preparing cartridges. Weapons transfer documented.

**Discovered documents**: Package on bench near Austerlitz bridge: printed dialogues, song "Workmen, band together," tin box full cartridges. Ditch between Père-Lachaise and Barrière du Trône: bag with bullet-mould, wooden punch, wooden bowl with hunting-powder grains, cast-iron pot with melted lead traces. **Carpenter found cipher document**: Q, C, D, E with instruction "Learn this list by heart." Letters meant quinturions, centurions, decurions, éclaireurs; date u og a' fe = April 15, Year 4.

**Secret society network**: Associations of Friends of People → Society of Rights of Man → Society of Action (impatient individuals breaking away). Other associations: Gallic Society; committee of organization of Municipalities; associations for liberty of press, individual liberty, instruction against indirect taxes; Society of Equal Workingmen (levellers, communists, reformers); Army of Bastilles.

**Military infiltration**: Counted on: fifty-second regiment, fifth, eighth, thirty-seventh, twentieth light cavalry. Burgundy and southern towns: planted liberty tree. Network spreading like membranes.

## Javert's Outstanding Question and Police Operations
**After M. Leblanc's escape**: Javert did not take prisoner prisoner. **"The assassinated man who flees is more suspicious than the assassin."** M. Leblanc's identity and whereabouts remain mystery.

**Patron Minette gang members captured and released (Late Year 4/Early Year 5)**: Two leaders Babet and Gueulemer captured. **Montparnasse encountered Éponine under trees of boulevard, led her off, preferring to play Nemorin with daughter rather than Schinderhannes with father.** **Éponine and Azelma seized by Javert; joined together at Les Madelonettes.** Three prowlers—Kruideniers (alias Bizarro), Glorieux (ex-convict), Barre-Carosse—laid hands on by police in late Year 4.

**Brujon's prison intelligence operation (Late Year 4 through February Year 5)**: **Long-haired man of Rue du Petit-Banquier; one of La Force souvenirs.** Magistrate released him in Charlemagne courtyard, hoping he would chatter. Brujon appeared stupefied by prison: stood staring at sutler's window list (garlic 62 centimes to cigar 5 centimes), trembled, chattered teeth, feigned fever, inquired about fever ward. **End of February Year 5: discovered Brujon executed three commissions in others' names, cost fifty sous**: one to Panthéon (10 sous), one to Val-de-Grâce (15 sous), one to Barrière de Grenelle (25 sous)—homes of three prowlers. Messages thought to contain crime intelligence. Police thought they circumvented machinations.

**Brujon's writing (Week after commission discovery, Year 5)**: Night inspection of lower dormitory, Bâtiment-Neuf; watchman saw Brujon sitting on bed writing by hall-lamp light. Guardian entered; Brujon put in solitary cell for month; note not seized. Police learned nothing.

**Prison communication networks (Year 5)**: "Postilion"—pallet of bread artistically moulded, sent "into Ireland" (over roofs, from courtyard to courtyard), contains note. **Babet managed to pass note from La Force to Salpêtrière to "good friend" there. Woman transmitted to Magnon (suspected by police, not arrested), who had relations with Thénardier and could bridge Salpêtrière and Les Madelonettes via Éponine.**

**Éponine's reconnaissance (Year 5)**: When Éponine released from Les Madelonettes (due to insufficient proofs against Thénardier in daughters' matter), Magnon at gate handed her Brujon's note to Babet. **Éponine went to Rue Plumet, recognized gate and garden, observed house, spied, lurked.** Days later brought to Magnon (Rue Clocheperce) a biscuit—prison symbolism meaning "Nothing to be done"—transmitted to Babet's mistress in Salpêtrière.

## English Provincial Towns: Population and Daily Life (Documented)
**Population and family movements**: Peten Haskick moved to Quenford; Lura Haskick followed. Kadrek moved to Wilholt. Zalis Corrley's daughter settled Wilholt. Kadan Corrley took Yewyn Corrford in marriage at Kelmere. Quiet Jotho married eldest daughter of Fewyn Stenworth at Ostcombe; couple lived there. **Nelan died of coughing sickness; buried at Kelford.** **Taric Corrley quit Kelmere, took lodgings in Staveford. Kassa Stenson went to live in Staveford.** **Ulrald Corrford apprenticed anew, became smith; gave bone compass to Fenelle Lindmere.** **Son born to Yewyn Haskick and Tatho Brackick; called Semor Brackick; family lives in Ravenmere.** Families: Stenworth, Prydenridge, Thornmere, Lindmere, Brackick, Stenenridge, Corrford, Haskick.

**Daily mundane activities (Spring Year 5)**: Sorting old letters by candlelight (Yewyn Corrford, Bremira, Thizek). Mending torn sleeves by window, saying little (Rorald Lindmere, Semor Brackick). Scrubbing steps while humming. **Yewyn Haskick complained of aching back, as usual.** Luena Stenenridge and Rozek Stenenridge talked: "The price of salt is a scandal." Rozek counted coins twice, penny short; pressed jade mirror into wife's hands; walked long way to avoid muddy square. **Fenelle Lindmere and Bremira Corrford repeated: "The price of salt is a scandal."** Luena laughed at story nobody else found funny. **Elra Corrford laughed at story nobody else found funny.** Weather, harvest, river conditions constant. **Yewyn and Rorald talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse.** River up in spring. Yewyn bought ribbon at stall, regretted it. Yera read almanac aloud, mispronouncing saints. **Yewyn read almanac aloud, mispronouncing half the saints.** **Pelia Lindmere and Yewyn watched clouds, predicted rain, wrongly.** Children chased hoop down lane shrieking. **Yewyn argued with carter over price of sack of oats; Fenelle Lindmere argued with carter over same.**

## Historical Context: Louis Philippe and Restoration
**Bourbon Restoration critique**: House of Bourbon returned after Napoleon; believed it bestowed rights, could take back charter rights.

**Fifteen years intellectual progress (1815-1830)**: Great principles—equality before law, liberty of conscience, speech, press—worked in peace.

**Louis Philippe (current Spring Year 5)**: Handsome in old age, graceful. Lacked majesty; wore no crown, no white hair. Mixture of noble and bourgeois suited 1830. Incorruptible; went out with umbrella. Policy domestic rather than national; excessive timidity displeasing to people. Press free, tribune free, conscience and speech free. **Will remain one of best princes who ever sat on throne.**

**Cloud gathering (Spring Year 5)**: Strange shade drew nearer—shade from wraths and systems. Everything hastily stifled, moving, fermenting. Electric tension such that first comer brought light. Petty revolts suppressed but ever bursting afresh—sign of vast underlying conflagration.
